questions.prompt: If A is \(2\times 3\) and B is \(3\times 4\), state the size of \(AB\).
questions.answer: For \(AB\) to be defined, the columns of A must match the rows of B. Here the inner sizes are both 3, so \(AB\) is defined. The outer sizes give the result: 2 rows and 4 columns. Therefore \(AB\) is \(2\times 4\).

Multiply each row of the matrix by the column vector. The first entry is \(1\cdot5+2\cdot6=17\). The second entry is \(3\cdot5+4\cdot6=39\). Therefore the product is \(\begin{pmatrix}17\\39\end{pmatrix}\).

Use row-column products. Top-left: \(2\cdot4\) + \(0\cdot2\) = 8. Top-right: \(2\cdot1\) + 0*(-2) = 2. Bottom-left: (-1)*4 + \(3\cdot2\) = 2. Bottom-right: (-1)*1 + 3*(-2) = -7. Therefore the product is \(\begin{pmatrix}8&2\\2&-7\end{pmatrix}\).

A is \(2\times 3\) and B is \(3\times 2\), so \(AB\) is defined and will be \(2\times 2\). Compute entries by row-column products. First row: \(1\cdot2\) + \(0\cdot0\) + \(2\cdot5\) = 12, and \(1\cdot1\) + \(0\cdot4\) + 2*(-2) = -3. Second row: (-1)*2 + \(3\cdot0\) + \(1\cdot5\) = 3, and (-1)*1 + \(3\cdot4\) + 1*(-2) = 9. Therefore \(AB\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}12&-3\\3&9\end{pmatrix}\).

Compute \(BA\) by multiplying B on the left by A on the right. Top-left: \(3\cdot1\) + \(0\cdot0\) = 3. Top-right: \(3\cdot2\) + \(0\cdot1\) = 6. Bottom-left: \(4\cdot1\) + \(5\cdot0\) = 4. Bottom-right: \(4\cdot2\) + \(5\cdot1\) = 13. Therefore \(BA\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}3&6\\4&13\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Show that matrix multiplication is not commutative for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Compute \(AB\) first: \(AB\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1&1\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1\\0\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1&0\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Compute \(BA\) next: \(BA\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 1 + 0\cdot 0&1\cdot 1 + 0\cdot 1\\1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 0&1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). Since \(AB\) and \(BA\) are different, matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

questions.prompt: Let A be \(3\times 2\), B be \(2\times 5\), and C be \(5\times 4\). State the size of \(ABC\).
questions.answer: First \(AB\) is defined because A has 2 columns and B has 2 rows. The product \(AB\) has size \(3\times 5\). Then (\(AB\))C is defined because \(AB\) has 5 columns and C has 5 rows. The final product has size \(3\times 4\). Therefore \(ABC\) is \(3\times 4\).
The product is a \(1\times 1\) matrix. Compute the single entry: x*2 + \(1\cdot3\) = 2x + 3. Set it equal to 11: 2x + 3 = 11. Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, so \(x=4\). Therefore \(x=4\).

questions.prompt: A learner computes \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\) by multiplying entries position by position. Explain why this is not a valid matrix product.
questions.answer: The first matrix has size \(1\times 3\) and the second matrix also has size \(1\times 3\). For a product \(AB\), the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. Here the inner sizes are 3 and 1, which do not match. Therefore the matrix product is not defined. The learner used entrywise multiplication, which is not matrix multiplication.

\(A^2\) means A multiplied by itself. Compute AA. Top-left: \(1\cdot1\) + \(2\cdot3\) = 7. Top-right: \(1\cdot2\) + \(2\cdot4\) = 10. Bottom-left: \(3\cdot1\) + \(4\cdot3\) = 15. Bottom-right: \(3\cdot2\) + \(4\cdot4\) = 22. Therefore \(A^2\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}7&10\\15&22\end{pmatrix}\).
